name: Patellar Tendinopathy
summary: Load-related pain at the patellar tendon, commonly at the inferior pole, in jumping and running athletes.

looksLike: Pain during jumping, landing, stairs or decline squat
redFlags: Acute pop with extensor mechanism failure
Inability to actively extend knee or perform straight-leg raise
Large traumatic effusion or suspected fracture
firstSteps: Reduce jump/sprint volume to tolerable level
Maintain strength with isometrics or reduced-range resistance
Explain that complete rest often reduces capacity

assess: Pain with decline squat or resisted knee extension

tests.name: Single-Leg Decline Squat
tests.purpose: Load the patellar tendon and reproduce familiar focal tendon pain.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Reduce jump/sprint volume to tolerable level
Maintain strength with isometrics or reduced-range resistance
Explain that complete rest often reduces capacity
dose: Spanish squat or knee-extension isometric: 5 x 30–45 seconds if tolerated
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Progress heavy slow resistance or eccentric-concentric loading
Introduce low-level energy-storage drills when strength tolerates
dose: Progress load when technique and next-day response acceptable
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Progress hopping, jumping, landing and sport-specific volume
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Hopping and jumping completed with acceptable symptoms
Full training volume and next-day recovery demonstrated

structures: Quadriceps mechanism and patellofemoral joint may contribute to differential
mechanism: Repeated high-rate tendon loading from jumping, sprinting or rapid training increase
classification: Persistent tendon pain with reduced load capacity; imaging severity does not equal pain severity
investigations: Usually clinical; ultrasound/MRI if uncertain, suspected tear or persistent symptoms despite rehabilitation.
Urgent imaging/referral for extensor mechanism failure.
manual: Manual therapy may address coexisting mobility issues but does not remodel tendon by itself.
modalities: Taping/straps may offer temporary symptom relief in selected athletes.
Passive modalities should not replace progressive tendon loading.
mistakes: Only eccentric decline squats for everyone
Using imaging to dictate symptoms or clearance
pearls: Progressive loading is the foundation; select isometric, isotonic and plyometric stages by capacity.
A tendon may remain structurally abnormal after function improves.

tests.name: Single-Leg Decline Squat
tests.purpose: Load the patellar tendon and reproduce familiar focal tendon pain.
tests.patientPosition: Stand on a decline board if available; perform controlled single-leg squat to tolerable depth.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Supports tendon-related pain; distinguish patellofemoral pain and extensor mechanism tear.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
